templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a participial opener
items.passage: Pumpkin toadlets, miniature frogs endemic to Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, leap readily but frequently tumble midair and crash on ______ the toadlets’ inner ears, a team led by biologist Richard Essner determined that the semicircular canals, which detect rotation, are too small to function reliably.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Pumpkin toadlets ... crash on landing” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the participial phrase “Examining the toadlets’ inner ears,” which describes its subject, “a team led by biologist Richard Essner,” and then gives the verb “determined.” A period is needed to separate the two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: The participial phrase belongs to the second independent clause, so the comma alone joins two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and the comma after “ears” then joins “a team ... determined” to the first clause.

C.why_wrong: “And” attaches the participial phrase to the first clause, which leaves “a team ... determined” joined to it with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science (herpetology, sensory biology). Band 6: a 5-word participial opener of the 3.4 / 886dc9f9 kind; splice, fused and added-and menu.

band7.why: aab74a3b / 886dc9f9 shape: a 5-word participial opener; the cue ('a team') sits inside the 6-word window and 'examining' cannot hang on the toadlets. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long participial opener
items.passage: Medellín’s Metrocable, a gondola line inaugurated in 2004, connects impoverished hillside neighborhoods in the Colombian city to its metro ______ neighborhoods served by the gondola with comparable ones it did not reach, epidemiologist Magdalena Cerdá’s team found that homicide rates declined far more where the gondola operated.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “to its metro system.” The second opens with the long participial phrase “Comparing neighborhoods served by the gondola with comparable ones it did not reach,” which describes its subject, “epidemiologist Magdalena Cerdá’s team”; the verb “found” follows. A period separates the two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “comparing ...” look like a description of the gondola line, but “epidemiologist Magdalena Cerdá’s team found” is a second independent clause joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation the first clause runs straight into the participial phrase, and the clause about Cerdá’s team is then joined with only a comma.

D.why_wrong: “And” links the participial phrase to the first clause, so the two independent clauses are still joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban policy, epidemiology). Band 6: a 13-word participial opener, the 73a6603c / 886dc9f9 range; no semicolon option, since a semicolon would also be correct here.

band7.why: 73a6603c / 1b97cce9 range: 13-word gerund-participial opener; it cannot plausibly modify 'metro system', so the splice shows by meaning before the subject arrives. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a past-participle opener
items.passage: In 1960, Brazilian artist Lygia Clark began producing her Bichos, a series of tabletop geometric ______ from flat aluminum plates articulated by hinges, the Bichos have no definitive form: participants are invited to manipulate them into configurations that Clark never prescribed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1960, Brazilian artist Lygia Clark began producing her Bichos, a series of tabletop geometric sculptures” is a complete sentence. “Assembled from flat aluminum plates articulated by hinges” describes the subject of the next sentence, “the Bichos,” whose verb is “have.” Only a period correctly separates the two independent clauses.

A.recipe: comma splice (opener read as a trailing modifier)
A.why_wrong: The participial phrase seems to describe “sculptures,” but “the Bichos have no definitive form” is then a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: “Sculptures assembled from ...” reads as one noun phrase, so the comma after “hinges” joins two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: “That were” turns the phrase into a clause describing “sculptures,” and the independent clause beginning “the Bichos have” is still joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: arts (sculpture). Band-7 checks: opener 8 words, a past participle that reads naturally as a modifier of clause 1's last noun (“sculptures”); the splice only shows at “the Bichos,” 8 words after the blank (cue outside a 6-word window); one-sentence run of 41 words; reasoning steps 3. No semicolon option.
band7_moves: opener of 8 words, a past participle that could modify clause 1's last noun
the comma, no-mark and that-were options all read as natural modifiers of “sculptures” until the subject arrives 8 words later

band7.why: a872c60a / 940ff6f7 shape and menu (period key, splice, glued, added 'that were'): an 8-word past-participle opener reads as a modifier of 'sculptures' until 'the Bichos have' arrives 9 words after the blank; one run of 41 words. Only C is grammatical.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening clause 2 (L; however, R)
items.passage: Many plants compete for scarce soil nutrients by producing additional roots whenever they detect a neighbor. Biologist Susan Dudley found that sea rocket, an annual plant of Great Lakes shorelines, responds this way to unrelated ______ when sea rocket seedlings shared containers with siblings, they invested less in root growth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Biologist Susan Dudley found that sea rocket ... responds this way to unrelated plants” and “when sea rocket seedlings shared containers with siblings, they invested less in root growth” are both independent clauses. “However” introduces the contrast in the second clause, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “however” leave two independent clauses joined with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation before “however,” the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, and “however” at the start of the second clause also needs a comma after it.

items.notes: Subject: science (plant ecology). Band 6: the adverb opens clause 2 and contrasts it with clause 1 (as `; rather,` in 3.5); three splice disguises, as in the band-6 adverb sets. No `, however;` option, so meaning never has to decide.

band7.why: '; however,' opening clause 2 with three splice disguises, the band-6 adverb set (a9e5b788, 3.29); no ', however;' option, so meaning never decides. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Supplementary adverb closing clause 1 (L, though; R)
items.passage: A mammal’s skull ordinarily stays the same size once the animal reaches maturity. The common shrew, an insectivore of Europe and northern Asia, is a striking ______ each autumn its skull and brain shrink before partially regrowing in spring, a cycle that may reduce its metabolic demands in winter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Though” contrasts the shrew with the claim in the previous sentence, so it belongs at the end of the first clause, set off by a comma. The second clause, “each autumn its skull and brain shrink ...,” explains why the shrew is an exception, and a semicolon joins the two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “though,” the two independent clauses are joined with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: “Though” would then introduce “each autumn its skull and brain shrink ...” as a concession, but the shrinking is the reason the shrew is an exception, not something that works against it.

C.why_wrong: “Though” would make the words after the semicolon a dependent clause, which cannot stand on its own after a semicolon.

items.notes: Subject: science (mammal physiology, Dehnel's phenomenon). Band-7 checks: adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; B is grammatical but wrong by meaning (concession), C is the semicolon-before-though pattern, A a splice, as in 5aa171de and 21e58a83; the deciding cue is in the previous sentence (outside the window); run 37 words; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1 and contrasts with the previous sentence
logic-wrong distractor (`, though` read as a subordinator gives a false concession)
semicolon-before-though option fails only once `though` is seen as a subordinator

fixes: sentence 1: 'stops growing' to 'stays the same size', so the autumn shrinking itself breaks the rule and B's concessive 'though' cannot be read as conceding the shrink while the regrowth carries the exception

band7.why: 21e58a83 / 5aa171de menu exactly: ', though;' closes clause 1 and answers sentence 1; B (subordinating 'though') is a clean logic-wrong distractor, since the shrinking and regrowth are the exception, not a concession against it; C leaves a dependent clause after a semicolon; A splices. Deciding cue in the previous sentence.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a list whose items contain commas
items.passage: A stone tablet inscribed in China in 1409 and subsequently erected in Galle, Sri Lanka, by the fleet of the Ming admiral Zheng He commemorates the expedition’s lavish donations with a text in three ______ addressed to the Buddha; Tamil, addressed to a Hindu deity; and Persian, addressed to Allah.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence is complete at “in three languages,” and what follows is a list naming those languages. A colon is used after a complete clause to introduce such a list.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the list that follows has no verb; the semicolons later in the sentence separate the list items.

C.why_wrong: The period makes the list a separate sentence with no verb, a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a colon, the names of the languages run directly into “three languages” with nothing to introduce the list.

items.notes: Subject: history (Ming voyages, Sri Lanka). Band 6: colon before a three-item list as in 3.22 and e7afd0a1, whose items carry their own commas, so the later semicolons tempt a semicolon at the blank. No lone dash option.

band7.why: c468db1c (3.22) / e7afd0a1 shape: colon before a three-item list whose items carry commas, the later semicolons tempting a semicolon at the blank. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (not a person) followed by a nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: In 2014, geochemist Graham Pearson’s team reported that a tiny crystal of the ______ which forms only under pressures found hundreds of kilometers underground, had reached the surface encased in a diamond and contained about 1.5 percent water, suggesting that Earth’s mantle holds vast amounts of water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Ringwoodite” identifies which mineral is meant, so it is essential to “the mineral” and takes no commas. The clause “which forms only under pressures found hundreds of kilometers underground” adds information about ringwoodite and is set off by a pair of commas; the second comma is already after “underground,” so the first goes after “ringwoodite.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma before “which,” the nonessential clause is left with only its closing comma, which then separates the subject “a tiny crystal” from its verb “had reached.”

C.why_wrong: The commas treat “ringwoodite” as extra information, but the name is what identifies the mineral.

D.why_wrong: The comma separates “the mineral” from its essential name, and no comma opens the clause that “underground,” closes.

items.notes: Subject: science (geochemistry). Band-7 checks: non-person restrictive appositive (“the mineral ringwoodite,” cf. 59a246dc's “the chemical compound aluminum oxide”) plus a second slot ruled by a different rule (opening comma of a which clause); the cue for that slot is the comma after “underground,” 10 words from the blank; run 45 words; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: restrictive appositive that is not a person
second slot set by a different rule (nonrestrictive clause after the name)
partner comma 10 words from the blank

band7.why: 59a246dc shape (non-person restrictive appositive 'the mineral ringwoodite') plus a second slot ruled by a different rule: the opening comma of the which clause, whose partner sits after 'underground', 10 words away. C (commas around the name) is CB's band-7 trap.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a descriptor and the name it identifies
items.passage: Ethio-jazz, a genre that combines the pentatonic scales of traditional Ethiopian music with the harmonic language and improvisational practices of American jazz, emerged in the late 1960s in recordings by Ethiopian ______ Mulatu Astatke, who had studied music in London, Boston, and New York.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Ethiopian vibraphonist” and the name “Mulatu Astatke” form one unit: the name identifies which vibraphonist is meant, so no punctuation separates the descriptor from the name.

A.why_wrong: The comma treats the name as extra information, but “Ethiopian vibraphonist,” with no article, cannot stand without the name it introduces.

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; “recordings by Ethiopian vibraphonist” is not one.

D.why_wrong: The dash separates the descriptor from the name, but “Ethiopian vibraphonist,” with no article, cannot stand without the name that identifies which vibraphonist is meant, so no punctuation belongs between them.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music). Band 6: plain title-plus-name item of the 3.11 kind (a comma after the name tempts a matching comma before it).

fixes: D why_wrong: rests on the descriptor needing its name (as in 3.11), not on the missing second dash

band7.why: 594b4a94 (3.11) shape: bare descriptor plus name, comma after the name tempting one before it; local. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: In 1946, Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy began constructing New Gourna, a village near Luxor intended to rehouse families residing among pharaonic tombs, employing the mud bricks and vaulted roofs of traditional Nubian ______ because many of those families resisted relocation, the settlement was never completed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1946, Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy began constructing New Gourna ... employing the mud bricks and vaulted roofs of traditional Nubian builders” and “because many of those families resisted relocation, the settlement was never completed” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “but” joins them and marks the contrast.

A.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation and no conjunction.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: When “but” joins two independent clauses this long, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (architecture). Plan cell asked for band 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials (band7/boundaries.md), so per WAVE.md it is written as a strong band 6: a 33-word clause 1 with an appositive and a participial tail, and clause 2 opening with a 7-word because-clause, so the second subject is 8 words from the blank.

band7.why: Plan asked 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials, so it stands as a strong band 6 (59094d87, 7ce4ee13): 33-word clause 1 and a because-clause before clause 2's subject, 8 words from the blank.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: Since settling in Hamburg in 1982, Japanese author Yoko Tawada has published novels, poetry, and essays in two ______ the Akutagawa Prize, Japan’s most coveted award for emerging writers, and the Kleist Prize, one of Germany’s most prestigious literary distinctions; and completed a doctorate in German literature.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things Tawada has done: written in two languages, received two prizes, and completed a doctorate. Because the items contain commas of their own, semicolons separate them, as the semicolon before “and completed” shows; a semicolon also belongs after “languages.”

A.why_wrong: A comma here does not match the semicolon that separates the second and third items, so the reader cannot tell where the items begin and end.

C.why_wrong: A colon would present the rest of the sentence as an explanation of “two languages,” but it is the next item in the list.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the first and second items run together.

items.notes: Subject: literature. Band 6: a verb-phrase series (aaa1907f and c49e946e shape, not b1's list of titles); item 1 holds its own list of three nouns, item 2 two appositives, and the revealing semicolon comes 21 words after the blank.

band7.why: c49e946e / aaa1907f verb-phrase series, blank closing item 1, revealing semicolon 21 words later. Band 6, as targeted (near the band-7 S5 recipe but single-rule options).

items.subtype: Comma pair around an interrupter after a conjunction
items.passage: Every June, four Quechua communities in Peru reconstruct the Q’eswachaka, a suspension footbridge over the Apurímac River. Villagers twist grass into cords ______ braid them into the cables and handrails of a replacement bridge.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: and, within just a few days,
and within just a few days,
and, within just a few days
and within just a few days—
items.explanation: “Within just a few days” interrupts the compound verb “twist ... and braid,” so it is set off by a pair of commas: one after “and” and one before “braid.”

B.why_wrong: The comma before “braid” has no partner, so it separates the verb from the rest of the sentence.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “and” opens the interrupting phrase, but nothing closes it.

D.why_wrong: A single dash with no partner cuts the verb “braid” off from the rest of the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history and culture (Inca engineering). Band 6, modelled on 3.12 (`and, in the process,`); the interrupter is a time phrase rather than b1's however pair. Length near 3.12 (32 words), the only hard model.

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 officials; fdb16e20 (3.12) shape and menu with a time phrase for 'in the process'. Band 6, as targeted.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: Researchers at Newcastle University investigated whether praying mantises, like humans, perceive depth by comparing the slightly different images from their two eyes. The team fitted mantises with miniature 3D glasses and projected simulated prey onto a ______ the insects struck only when the stereoscopic illusion placed the prey within reach.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The team fitted mantises with miniature 3D glasses and projected simulated prey onto a screen” and “the insects struck only when ...” are both independent clauses. A comma and the coordinating conjunction “and” join them.

A.why_wrong: When “and” joins two independent clauses of this length, a comma is needed before it.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: science (insect vision). Medium: clause 1 itself contains a compound verb joined by “and,” so the student must see that “the insects struck” starts a new clause.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: The Garima Gospels, two illuminated manuscripts kept at a monastery in northern Ethiopia, were long assumed to date from around the eleventh ______ radiocarbon dating of their pages later indicated that they were made between the fourth and seventh centuries, placing them among the oldest illustrated Christian books in existence.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The Garima Gospels ... were long assumed to date from around the eleventh century” and “radiocarbon dating of their pages later indicated ...” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “but” joins them and signals the contrast between the old assumption and the new dates.

A.why_wrong: A comma is needed before “but” when it joins two independent clauses this long.

C.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “but”; it separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation or conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: history (manuscripts, Ethiopia). Medium: 1.31-style option set with `, but,` in place of the plain splice.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Archaeologists long wondered what tall cylindrical jars from Pueblo Bonito, a great house in New Mexico’s Chaco Canyon, had held. In 2009, anthropologist Patricia Crown found that residue on fragments of the jars contained theobromine, a compound present in ______ then, no evidence of chocolate drinking had turned up north of Mexico.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence about Crown’s finding ends with “a compound present in cacao.” “Until then” is a short introductory phrase that opens the next independent clause, whose subject is “no evidence.” A period separates the two independent clauses.

A.why_wrong: The comma joins two independent clauses, with “until then” attached to the first.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “until then” seems to modify “cacao,” and the two independent clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: “And” without a comma does not properly join two independent clauses, and it leaves “until then” unclear.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology of the US Southwest). Medium: 2-word opener after the period, as in 2.7 and 2.9.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: The twelfth-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Tufayl explored the capacities of unaided human reason in his philosophical novel Hayy ibn ______ a boy who, raised by a gazelle on an uninhabited island, deduces the principles of natural science and philosophy entirely on his own.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause ends with the title “Hayy ibn Yaqzan.” The participial phrase “imagining a boy who ...” is a supplementary element describing how Ibn Tufayl explored human reason, so a comma separates it from the main clause.

B.why_wrong: The words after the semicolon have no subject or finite verb of their own, so they cannot stand as an independent clause.

C.why_wrong: “Imagining a boy who ...” has no main verb, so it cannot be a sentence.

D.why_wrong: “And” suggests that a second action parallel to “explored” follows, but “imagining ...” is a participial phrase, not a verb that can share the subject “Ibn Tufayl.”

items.notes: Subject: literature and philosophy. Medium: trailing -ing phrase after a long main clause, as in 2.26; the phrase holds its own comma-set interrupter.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory participial phrase
items.passage: Paradise tree snakes of Southeast Asia glide between treetops by flattening their bodies. Recording the snakes with motion-capture cameras as they launched from a platform inside a four-story ______ team led by biologist Jake Socha determined that the snakes’ midair undulations prevent them from tumbling.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Recording the snakes ... inside a four-story arena” is an introductory participial phrase, not a complete sentence. A comma separates it from the main clause that follows, whose subject is “a team led by biologist Jake Socha” and whose verb is “determined.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the introductory phrase has no subject or main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period turns the introductory phrase into a sentence fragment.

D.why_wrong: “And” would join the introductory phrase to the main clause as if both were clauses, but the phrase has no subject or main verb.

items.notes: Subject: science (biomechanics). Medium: a 16-word introductory phrase with an embedded as-clause, so the main subject is far from the start of the sentence.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: In the ultimatum game, one participant proposes how to divide a sum of money, and a second participant accepts the proposal or rejects it, leaving both empty-handed. The Machiguenga horticulturalists whom anthropologist Joseph Henrich recruited to play the game in the Peruvian ______ made low offers, yet their counterparts seldom rejected them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “The Machiguenga horticulturalists whom anthropologist Joseph Henrich recruited to play the game in the Peruvian Amazon,” and its verb is “made.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.

A.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject from its verb, “made.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; the words before it are only the subject.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the words before it have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics, anthropology). Medium: 16-word subject with a relative clause and a place phrase before the verb, as in 2.3.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: German-born Venezuelan artist Gego transformed the line into a three-dimensional presence in series such as Reticulárea, an immersive web of interconnected wire first exhibited in Caracas in ______ Troncos, cylindrical columns built from metal rods; and Dibujos sin papel (Drawings without Paper), constructions in which wire substitutes for pencil lines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three series, each followed by a description set off by a comma. Because the items contain commas, semicolons separate them, as the semicolon before “and Dibujos sin papel” shows. A semicolon is needed after “1969” to end the first item.

A.why_wrong: A comma here would not match the semicolon used between the second and third items, so the items would be hard to tell apart.

C.why_wrong: A colon would present “Troncos” as an explanation of the first item rather than as the next item in the list.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the first item runs directly into the second.

items.notes: Subject: arts (sculpture). Medium: single-slot complex series with the blank closing item 1, as in 2.16.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: The Dunhuang Star Chart, a paper scroll produced in China during the Tang dynasty, is the oldest complete star atlas known from any civilization. Depicting more than 1,300 stars, it was discovered in 1900 among thousands ______ manuscripts concealed inside a Buddhist cave temple.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Of manuscripts” is a prepositional phrase: “manuscripts” is the object of the preposition “of.” No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; it cannot separate a preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: The comma separates the preposition “of” from its object.

D.why_wrong: The dash has no role here and separates the preposition from its object.

items.notes: Subject: history (Chinese astronomy, Mogao Caves). Easy: preposition-object boundary, four distinct marks.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Ghanaian philosopher Kwasi Wiredu called for the “conceptual decolonization” of African thought. He urged African philosophers to ______ concepts such as “truth” and “mind,” which had reached them through colonial education, by asking whether those concepts made sense in African languages such as his native Akan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Concepts such as ‘truth’ and ‘mind’” is the direct object of the verb “reexamine.” No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; “He urged African philosophers to reexamine” is incomplete without its object.

B.why_wrong: The comma separates the verb from its object.

D.why_wrong: The dash separates the verb from its object and has no partner.

items.notes: Subject: philosophy. Easy: verb-object boundary as in 1.15 and 1.16.

items.subtype: Direct question: inverted word order and a question mark
items.passage: In 2019, researchers reported that Atlantic puffins in Wales and Iceland had been filmed scratching their bodies with small sticks, the first documented instance of tool use among seabirds. The discovery raised a new question: How ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: did the puffins learn this behavior.
did the puffins learn this behavior?
items.explanation: After the colon, “How” begins a direct question, so the helping verb “did” comes before the subject (“did the puffins learn”) and the sentence ends with a question mark.

A.why_wrong: A direct question beginning with “How” needs the helping verb before the subject, not statement word order.

B.recipe: question errors (direct question ends with a period)
B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question ends with a question mark.

C.recipe: question errors (statement order and a period)
C.why_wrong: This is neither a correctly formed question nor a complete statement: “How the puffins learned this behavior” cannot stand as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: science (animal behavior). Easy: direct question after a colon, as in 1.18 (b1 used an embedded why-question).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses with a comma and a coordinating conjunction
items.passage: Biologists in Japan have found that the sea slug Elysia marginata can detach its head from its body at the ______ the head subsequently regenerates an entirely new body, heart included, within approximately three weeks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Biologists in Japan have found that the sea slug ... can detach its head from its body at the neck” and “the head subsequently regenerates an entirely new body ...” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by “and” joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma is needed before “and” when it joins two independent clauses of this length.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “and”; it separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: science (regeneration). Easy: clause 2 opens with its subject right after the blank.

items.subtype: Commas between items of a simple series
items.passage: Hogeweyk, a gated village that opened in 2009 in Weesp, the Netherlands, was designed specifically for residents with advanced dementia. They occupy small shared households and can wander freely through streets and courtyards that contain a ______ a restaurant, and a theater.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A supermarket,” “a restaurant,” and “a theater” are three items in a simple series. A comma separates the first item from the second, matching the comma after “restaurant.”

A.why_wrong: Semicolons separate list items only when the items contain commas; these do not.

B.why_wrong: A colon would present the rest of the list as an explanation of “a supermarket.”

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first two items of the series run together.

items.notes: Subject: social science (elder care, urban design). Easy: blank after item 1 of three, as in 1.25 and 1.12, so the serial-comma question never arises.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing such as phrase
items.passage: Nüshu, a script once used exclusively by women, developed over centuries in Jiangyong County in China’s Hunan Province. Women used Nüshu in letters and songs and wrote or embroidered its characters on everyday objects exchanged between sworn sisters or between mothers and ______ as fans and handkerchiefs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Such as fans and handkerchiefs” gives examples of the “everyday objects” mentioned earlier, not of daughters, so it is a supplementary phrase at the end of the sentence and is set off with a comma.

A.why_wrong: The words after the semicolon are a phrase, not an independent clause.

B.why_wrong: “Such as fans and handkerchiefs” has no subject or verb and cannot stand as a sentence.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the examples seem to describe “daughters” rather than the objects.

items.notes: Subject: language and writing systems. Easy: such-as tail whose examples belong to a noun earlier in the sentence, as in 1.11, so the no-comma version misreads.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around a which clause
items.passage: In 2021, primatologists reported that two wild female bonobos had adopted infants from neighboring communities. The adoptions, which occurred at Wamba, a research site in the Democratic Republic of the ______ were the first such cases documented among wild great apes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “adoptions” opens the supplementary clause “which occurred at Wamba, a research site in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.” A comma after “Congo” closes it before the verb “were.”

B.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the supplementary clause runs into the main verb “were.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon would separate the subject “The adoptions” from its verb “were.”

D.why_wrong: “And” makes “were the first such cases” part of the which clause, so the sentence has no main verb for “The adoptions.”

items.notes: Subject: science (primatology). Easy: closing comma of a which clause that holds an appositive, partner 14 words back, as in 1.10.
